parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A woman phones an arts centre about an evening photography course.
script: Good afternoon, City Arts Centre, Mark speaking.
Hi. I'm calling about the evening photography courses.
Yes, we have two this term: portrait photography and landscape photography.
I was hoping to do portrait.
I'm sorry, portrait is already full. There's a waiting list, but there are twelve people on it already.
Oh. Then I'll go for landscape. That's probably more my style anyway. I love being outdoors.
Great. Let me take your details. Your name?
Amina Hossain. That's H, O, double S, A, I, N.
Thank you. The landscape course starts on Tuesday the ninth of September. Originally it was the second, but the teacher's away that week.
That's fine. Which room is it in?
Room B12, on the first floor. Not B21. People often mix them up.
B12. And how much does it cost?
It's a hundred and twenty pounds for ten weeks. That includes printing for the final exhibition.
Do I need an expensive camera?
Not at all. Any digital camera is fine, or even a smartphone. The teacher's very keen to show what phones can do.
That's good, because I only have my phone. Who's the teacher?
Grace Okafor. She's a professional landscape photographer. That's O, K, A, F, O, R.
Is the course all in the classroom?
No, there's a field trip in week five. It was going to be to the forest park, but this year Grace has chosen the coast, because of the sunrise views.
Lovely. Do I need any other equipment?
Just one thing: a tripod. They're quite cheap, and you'll need one for low-light shots.
OK. And where is the exhibition held?
At the end of term, students' best photos are displayed in the café on the ground floor. Not the main gallery, which is booked for a professional show.
And one last question for our records. How did you hear about the course?
I heard an advertisement on the radio.
Ah, good to know. We've only just started advertising there. Thank you, Amina.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A park ranger welcomes visitors to a national park.
script: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Green Ridge National Park. I'm Lucy, one of the rangers here, and I'd like to give you some information before you set off.

First, a little history. The park was created in 1972. Many people assume it was set up for tourism or to protect wildlife, but in fact the main reason was to protect the forest that supplies drinking water to the towns below. Tourism came later.

A few rules. Dogs are welcome as long as they're on a lead, and there are barbecue areas near the car park. But please don't pick any plants or flowers. Some of them are extremely rare and are found nowhere else.
A word about the weather. Mornings are usually clear, but mist can come down very quickly, especially in the afternoons, so please keep an eye on the sky.
Here at the visitor centre we have a café and toilets, and you can hire binoculars. We used to hire out bicycles as well, but we stopped last year.
Now, the trails. The Waterfall Trail is just two kilometres long and fully paved, so it's suitable for wheelchairs and pushchairs.
The Ridge Trail is seven kilometres. It's steep in places, but from the top you get the best views of the lake.
The Forest Loop, which is five kilometres, goes through the oldest part of the forest. In spring, look out for orchids. We have several species that grow only in this park.

Finally, the Summit Path is twelve kilometres there and back, and it's only for experienced walkers. You must carry a map, because the phone signal is unreliable, and please start before nine a.m., so that you're back down before the afternoon mist arrives.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students, Nadia and Omar, plan an app for their design project.
script: So, Nadia, we have to choose the focus for our app design project.
I've been thinking about it. Most language apps are aimed at complete beginners, but there's very little for intermediate learners who want to improve their speaking.
That's true. When I was learning Spanish, I could read quite well, but I froze whenever I had to speak.
What did you think of the survey results from our classmates?
I was surprised how many said they'd pay for an app. More than half. I'd expected students to want everything free.
The main feature I'd like is conversation practice with a virtual partner.
Agreed, but it should give feedback on mistakes at the end of the conversation, not interrupt you in the middle. That's what annoyed me about other apps.
For the presentation to Dr Lee, do we need a working prototype?
She said a design mock-up is enough this time. The prototype comes next term.
And what about the name? I like TalkTrail.
Let's not decide yet. We should check whether another app is already using it.
Good idea. Now, features. I think we should include a daily streak, so users are motivated to come back every day.
Sure. And I'd like users to be able to choose topics, like travel, work or hobbies, so the conversations feel relevant to them.
Nice. Another thing: users could record themselves and compare their pronunciation with a native speaker's.
Maybe. For the design, I'd keep the colours very simple. Too many options confuse people.
And one more thing. I'd like to test the app with real users from the international students' society before we finish.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecture about mapping the ocean floor.
script: Good morning. Today I want to talk about something that surprises many people: how little we know about the shape of the ocean floor. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of our own seabed. As recently as 2017, only around six percent of the ocean floor had been mapped in high resolution.

The earliest way of measuring depth was very simple. Sailors lowered a rope with a heavy weight attached until it hit the bottom. It was slow, and the results were often inaccurate, because currents pulled the rope sideways.

A major advance came in the 1920s with echo sounding. A ship sends a pulse of sound down to the seabed and measures how long it takes for the echo to return. Since we know the speed of sound in water, we can calculate the depth.

One of the most important figures in this history is Marie Tharp, an American geologist. In the 1950s, women were not allowed on research ships, so Tharp worked from data collected by her male colleagues. Plotting thousands of measurements by hand, she noticed a deep valley, or rift, running down the centre of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. At first her colleagues dismissed the idea, but her discovery provided crucial evidence for the theory of continental drift, the idea that the continents slowly move apart.

Today, ships use multibeam sonar, which sends out a fan of sound beams and maps a wide strip of seabed at once, rather than a single point. Satellites also help. Underwater mountains have a gravitational pull, which creates tiny bumps in the sea surface, and satellites can measure these. However, satellite maps are low resolution, so ships remain essential.

An international project called Seabed 2030 aims to map the entire ocean floor by the end of this decade. Why does it matter? Accurate maps make navigation safer, and they're needed for laying the internet cables that carry most of the world's data. They also help scientists model how tsunamis travel, which improves warning systems.
There are concerns, though. Some people fear that detailed maps will make it easier for companies to begin deep-sea mining, which could destroy habitats we have barely begun to study.

passages.title: The Banyan Tree
paragraphs: Few trees are as closely tied to the culture of South Asia as the banyan. It is the national tree of India, it appears in ancient Hindu and Buddhist texts, and for centuries village councils have met in its shade. Its English name comes from 'banias', the Indian traders whom Portuguese and British visitors observed doing business beneath its branches.

The banyan is a type of fig, and its life begins in an unusual way. Birds or bats eat its fruit and deposit the seeds high in the branches of another tree. There the seed germinates, sending roots down towards the ground. Once these roots reach the soil, they thicken rapidly and gradually surround the host tree's trunk. Over many decades, the banyan may completely enclose its host, which eventually dies, a habit that has earned some fig species the name 'strangler figs'.

The banyan's most distinctive feature is its aerial roots. These grow down from the horizontal branches, and when they reach the ground they become thick, woody pillars that support the branches as they extend outwards. In this way, a single tree can spread across an enormous area. The Great Banyan in the botanic garden near Kolkata covers around 18,000 square metres, roughly the size of two and a half football pitches, and has more than 3,600 aerial roots. Its original trunk was damaged by a fungal infection and removed in 1925, but the tree has continued to grow.

Banyans are of great ecological importance. Because they produce fruit throughout the year rather than in a single season, they are a reliable food source for many birds, bats and monkeys, especially at times when other food is scarce. One study in southern India recorded more than 70 species of birds feeding on a single banyan over the course of a year.

The relationship between the banyan and its pollinator is particularly remarkable. Like all figs, the banyan's flowers are hidden inside the fruit, and they can only be pollinated by a tiny wasp, a species that has evolved alongside the tree for millions of years. The female wasp enters the fruit through a narrow opening, pollinates the flowers and lays her eggs. Neither the tree nor the wasp can reproduce without the other.

Today, many old banyans are threatened by road-widening schemes and urban development. In some cities, citizens' groups have campaigned successfully to protect individual trees, and several Indian states have introduced special legal protection for very old trees. Some environmentalists have also pointed out that the banyan cools its surroundings: temperatures beneath a large canopy can be several degrees lower than in nearby streets, which makes it valuable for cities facing increasingly hot summers.

passages.title: Rewilding
paragraphs: In the Oostvaardersplassen, a nature reserve built on land reclaimed from the sea in the Netherlands, herds of wild horses, red deer and cattle graze across open grassland. None of these animals is fed or managed in the usual sense; the idea is that, left largely alone, they will shape the landscape much as their wild ancestors once did. The reserve was strongly influenced by the Dutch ecologist Frans Vera, who argued that Europe's prehistoric landscape was not a dense forest, as many believed, but a mixture of woodland and open grassland kept open by large grazing animals.

The term 'rewilding' is used in many different ways, but at its core it means restoring natural processes rather than managing land to achieve a fixed result. Traditional conservation often focuses on protecting particular species or habitats, such as a meadow rich in wildflowers that must be cut every summer to keep it that way. Rewilding, by contrast, tries to step back and let nature decide. The British writer George Monbiot has argued that rewilding should not try to return an ecosystem to any particular earlier state, but should allow it to find its own way.

Large animals play a central role. The American biologists Michael Soulé and Reed Noss argued in 1998 that effective rewilding requires three things: large core areas of protected land, corridors connecting them, and carnivores. Predators such as wolves, they argued, control the numbers and behaviour of grazing animals, preventing overgrazing and allowing trees and shrubs to regenerate.

The best-known example comes from Yellowstone National Park in the United States, where wolves were reintroduced in 1995 after an absence of seventy years. In the following years, researchers reported that elk numbers fell and that elk avoided valleys where they could easily be trapped, allowing willow and aspen trees to recover along riverbanks. Some even claimed that the wolves had changed the course of rivers by stabilising their banks. More recent research has suggested that this account is too simple: the ecologist Arthur Middleton has pointed out that drought, hunting by humans and the return of bears also reduced elk numbers.

In Europe, rewilding has often happened by accident. Since the 1960s, millions of hectares of farmland in southern and eastern Europe have been abandoned as rural populations moved to cities. Forests have returned, and with them animals such as wild boar, deer and, increasingly, wolves and bears. The ecologist Henrique Pereira has suggested that the further abandonment of farmland expected in the coming decades will create an unprecedented opportunity for wildlife.

Not everyone welcomes these changes. Farmers whose sheep are killed by wolves are often fiercely opposed to their return, and in rural communities rewilding can feel like a project imposed by city-dwelling environmentalists. In the Oostvaardersplassen, thousands of animals starved during a harsh winter in 2018, leading to public protests, and the authorities were forced to begin reducing herd numbers. Supporters argued that such deaths are natural; critics replied that a fenced reserve, from which animals cannot migrate, is not a natural system at all.

passages.title: The Restless Mind
paragraphs: Human beings are, by the standards of most animals, extraordinarily restless. Within tens of thousands of years of leaving Africa, our species had reached almost every habitable part of the planet, crossing deserts, mountain ranges and open ocean. Today, millions of people travel for pleasure to places they have never seen, try unfamiliar foods and take up hobbies with no obvious practical value. What drives this appetite for the new, and why do some people seem to have so much more of it than others?

Psychologists use the term 'novelty seeking' to describe a tendency to pursue new and intense experiences. It was identified in the 1980s by the psychiatrist Robert Cloninger as one of four basic dimensions of temperament, and it can be measured with questionnaires asking, for example, whether people enjoy exploring unfamiliar places or quickly grow bored with routine. Scores vary widely, and they appear to be partly inherited: studies of twins suggest that genes account for perhaps forty percent of the differences between individuals.

Much attention has focused on dopamine, a chemical messenger in the brain associated with motivation and reward. Brain-imaging studies show that the dopamine system responds strongly to new things, even before we know whether they will be pleasant. In one experiment at University College London, volunteers were shown a series of images, some familiar and some new; the reward area of the brain was more active for the new images, even though the images themselves had no value. The researchers concluded that novelty is, in a sense, its own reward: it encourages us to explore in case something useful turns out to be there.

In the 1990s, some researchers claimed to have found a link between novelty seeking and a particular version of a gene involved in the dopamine system. This version was found more frequently in populations whose ancestors had migrated long distances, and some writers popularised it as an 'explorer gene'. Later, larger studies, however, failed to confirm a strong link, and most geneticists now believe that complex traits like novelty seeking are influenced by hundreds of genes, each with a tiny effect. I think the explorer-gene story is a warning about how readily a simple, attractive explanation can spread beyond the evidence.

From an evolutionary perspective, the value of exploration seems clear. An animal that never leaves its familiar territory may miss better sources of food; one that constantly wanders may waste energy and run into danger. Ecologists call this the 'explore–exploit trade-off', and the same problem appears in computer science, where programs must decide whether to try new options or stick with ones known to work well. A population containing individuals with different tendencies may be better able to cope with changing conditions than one in which everybody behaves alike.

Novelty seeking is often described in negative terms, and linked to impulsiveness, risk-taking and addiction. There is some truth in this: high scorers are more likely to gamble or drive dangerously. But I believe this emphasis is misleading. When the trait is combined with persistence and self-control, it is associated with creativity, entrepreneurship and resilience. Cloninger's own research found that people who scored highly on novelty seeking, and also on persistence and cooperativeness, reported some of the highest levels of wellbeing in his samples.

Our appetite for the new also changes across the lifespan. Novelty seeking typically peaks in adolescence and declines steadily with age, which may help to explain why teenagers are more willing to take risks. Yet the decline is not inevitable. Older adults who continue to travel, learn and meet new people appear to maintain better cognitive health, although it is difficult to establish whether these activities protect the brain or simply reflect the habits of people whose brains are already healthier.

For individuals, the practical lesson may be that novelty is most valuable when it is chosen with care. Travel that challenges our assumptions, or skills that stretch our abilities, can provide the stimulation the brain seems to need, while a life of constant change without direction may leave us exhausted. The restless mind that carried our ancestors across continents is still with us; the task is to give it somewhere worthwhile to go.

task1.text: The bar chart below shows the average number of hours per day that people in four age groups spent looking at screens in 2015 and 2025. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
model: The bar chart compares the average number of hours per day that people in four age groups spent looking at screens in 2015 and 2025.

Overall, screen time increased in every age group over the decade, and teenagers saw both the largest rise and the highest figure by 2025. The oldest group consistently spent the least time on screens.

In 2015, people aged 19 to 30 had the highest daily screen time, at 5 hours, slightly more than teenagers, at 4.5 hours. Adults aged 31 to 50 averaged 3.5 hours, while those over 50 spent just 2 hours a day in front of a screen.

By 2025, teenagers had overtaken young adults, as their daily screen time rose by 2.5 hours to reach 7 hours. The figure for 19 to 30-year-olds also grew, to 6.5 hours. The two older groups each saw an increase of 1.5 hours, reaching 5 hours for people aged 31 to 50 and 3.5 hours for those over 50.

task2.text: Some people prefer to visit many different countries for short periods, while others prefer to spend a long time getting to know one place. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Write at least 250 words.
model: With cheaper flights and easier visas, travellers today have more choice than ever about how to spend their holidays. Some like to see as many countries as possible on a single trip, while others would rather stay in one place for weeks. Although both approaches have merits, I believe that spending longer in one place usually offers a richer experience.

Visiting several countries in a short time has obvious attractions. For people with limited holiday time, it is an efficient way to see famous sights and compare different cultures. A two-week tour of Southeast Asia, for example, might include temples in Cambodia, beaches in Thailand and food markets in Vietnam. This variety can be exciting, and it helps travellers decide which places they would like to return to in the future.

On the other hand, those who prefer to stay in one place argue that fast travel is often superficial. Much of the time is spent in airports, buses and hotel queues, and visitors rarely move beyond the main tourist areas. By contrast, someone who spends a month in a single town can learn some of the language, make friends with local people and understand daily life in a way that a short visit never allows. Slower travel is also less tiring and generally better for the environment, since it involves fewer flights.

In my opinion, the second approach is more rewarding. The most memorable travel experiences tend to come from conversations and unexpected moments rather than from ticking off famous landmarks, and these need time.
In conclusion, while visiting many countries can be exciting and efficient, I believe that getting to know one place well leads to deeper understanding and more meaningful memories.

speaking.cue:
Describe something new that you tried for the first time.
You should say:
- what it was
- when and where you tried it
- who you were with
and explain how you felt about it.
speaking.cueModel: I'd like to talk about the first time I went camping in the hills, which was in Bandarban, in the south-east of Bangladesh, about a year ago. A university friend of mine had been several times, and she persuaded three of us to join her for a long weekend. I'd always stayed in hotels before, so sleeping in a tent on a hillside was a completely new experience for me. We hiked for about five hours on the first day, through forest and past small villages, and it was much harder than I'd expected, especially on the steep parts. When we finally reached the campsite, we set up our tents, cooked rice and lentils over a small fire, and watched the sun go down over the valley. That evening was unforgettable. There were no city lights, so the sky was full of stars, and we just sat and talked for hours. At first, I felt a bit nervous, because I'm not used to being so far from everything, and the noises at night were quite strange. But by the next morning, when I woke up to see clouds below us in the valley, I felt incredibly calm and proud of myself. It made me want to try more things that take me out of my comfort zone.
